title: Things That Help: “I Can't Fix Everything, Or Sometimes Anything”
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. relays a story from third-grade teacher Beth Sheehan, who, exhausted eleven days into a remote-learning school year, went home mid-day and slept, waking with the realization: 'I can't fix everything, or sometimes anything.' Stuart treats the line as a proverb — a small, portable truth that counters the savior-complex tendency common among conscientious teachers to feel personally responsible for outcomes beyond their control. He pairs it with a complementary proverb about how much genuinely does lie within a teacher's control and can matter enormously, arguing that no single proverb captures the whole of reality and that wisdom literature is full of statements that seem to contradict yet are really facets of one diamond. The short piece ends with a practical suggestion: write down whatever line is currently carrying you and post it somewhere visible, as Stuart has done with an index card taped beneath his monitor.
points: Beth Sheehan's proverb, 'I can't fix everything, or sometimes anything,' functions as an antidote to the savior complex that drives many teachers toward unsustainable overwork.
Stuart pairs that proverb with its complement — that what a teacher does control can have enormous, generational impact — to avoid tipping into fatalism.
No single proverb captures the whole of reality; wisdom traditions deliberately hold seemingly contradictory truths together as facets of one diamond rather than as contradictions to resolve.
A simple physical practice — writing a helpful line on an index card and posting it somewhere visible — turns an abstract insight into a daily, repeated reminder.
quotes: I am teaching remotely in a Title I school and I am exhausted after 11 days. Our families have been slammed by this, and I had been killing myself trying to help them manage, trying to make sure they had what they needed, trying to connect.
That line of Beth's made me laugh: "I can't fix everything, or sometimes anything." It still gives me delight. Why? Because it's incontrovertible.
For those of us with would-be savior complexes, Beth's proverb is an amulet; it can keep off the mind-killers of unchecked self-reliance and ego assertion.

An overwhelming array of evidence — from sophisticated studies to commonplace classroom anecdotes — demonstrate how the briefest of classroom experiences — single comments from a teacher, single lessons on depression — can shift the trajectory of a student's life.

You'll never find a proverb that works 100% of the time. That's why books of wisdom (e.g., the Hebrew book of Proverbs) contain statements that seem to contradict one another. They're not contradictory; they're facets of a single diamond.
